claims.text: The initial material is a tungsten-based high-entropy alloy used as an intermediate layer in plasma-facing reactor components.
Conventional additive manufacturing involves rapid solidification that can reduce structural stability.
The intervention consists of forging at 900–1200 °C with intermediate cool-down intervals.
The forging is followed by tailored annealing intended to promote partial recrystallization and optimize nanoprecipitate distribution.
Heat treatment near 900 °C can induce recrystallization-related microstructural and mechanical changes in an additively manufactured high-entropy alloy.
The treatment will produce a partially recrystallized matrix.
The treatment will produce a refined, coherent nanoprecipitate network.
The resulting microstructure will avoid excessive grain-boundary density.
High-temperature forging reduces defect density.
High-temperature forging refines the alloy microstructure.
Controlled annealing promotes nanoprecipitate formation.
The nanoprecipitate network reduces heat-carrier scattering.
Reduced grain-boundary scattering improves thermal conductivity.
The tuned nanoprecipitate network preserves structural integrity, strength, and ductile performance.
Compared with conventionally processed samples, treated samples will have higher thermal conductivity.
Compared with conventionally processed samples, treated samples will retain comparable yield strength.
Compared with conventionally processed samples, treated samples will retain comparable ductility.
The benefits will hold at 900–1200 °C under high mechanical loads representative of plasma-facing reactor operation.
Processing outside the specified temperature regime may fail to produce the desired thermal and structural performance.
Current intermediate-layer processing prioritizes mechanical stability without specifically targeting enhanced thermal transport.

contradictions.description: The mediator emphasizes minimizing excessive grain-boundary density, while the mechanism says forging refines the microstructure; grain refinement ordinarily implies more grain-boundary area unless subsequent recrystallization or grain growth is specified quantitatively.
